name: Carlos Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a cardboard box plant, on the corrugator. That's the long machine that glues the wavy paper between two flat sheets to make board, about a hundred metres of rollers and steam. I'm on the wet end, feeding the paper reels and watching the glue and the heat, and if it goes wrong you get warped board and a very angry shift manager. It's hot, loud and the steam makes your shirt stick to you all year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sixteen years, since before Nikolai was born. What keeps me is it's close, ten minutes on the bike, and I know that machine like an old dog, I know its moods. There's nothing much else around here since the shoe factory went, so you don't go looking. I don't use any of this AI on my phone, my son tried to show me once and I told him I've got enough things talking to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, good, one less thing. Probably not say much at all, to be honest, it's not something we talk about over lunch. We talk about football and the price of diesel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means nothing changes, and nothing changing suits me. The boxes still need making, the online shopping still needs boxes. I'm not a man who looks for trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Go to work, come home, fix the fence I've been meaning to fix. Maybe ask for a few extra shifts before Christmas, we always need it in December.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relieved, if anything, but I wasn't losing sleep before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the money side feel at home in a normal year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena, my wife, she worries about money, I worry about it less, I think it works out. We've got almost nothing in the bank, but we've always got through. Her pharmacy hours went down last year, that was harder than any of this computer stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the plant changed much in your sixteen years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They did the stacker at the end of the line about six years ago, now it piles the sheets itself. Two jobs went, but both lads went to the other shift. Nobody got thrown out, so we got used to it.

S0.say: Fine, good, one less thing, though it's not really a lunch-table topic. At lunch they talk about football and the price of diesel.
S0.think: Nothing changing suits him, since boxes still need making for all the online shopping. He's not a man who looks for trouble.
S0.do: Carries on going to work and fixing things at home. Asks for a few extra shifts before Christmas, as the family always needs extra money in December.
S0.feel: Fine and a little relieved, though he wasn't losing sleep before.
S0.quote: Two jobs went, but both lads went to the other shift. Nobody got thrown out, so we got used to it.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is settled and unbothered in the plateau picture, trusting that boxes will always be needed. He plays down money worries his wife feels more sharply. The last automation at his plant moved people rather than firing them, which shapes his trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies have to keep up or they close, and then we're all out. I wouldn't make a fuss in public. You don't want to be the one the bosses remember as trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the wet end is the kind of thing a computer could watch better than me, the temperatures and the glue. I'm good, but I'm not the best, I'm somewhere in the middle. If they cut two out of five, I don't know which side of the line I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and see what they actually do, there's no point panicking over a rumour. We'd stop the satellite TV and Elena would want to stop eating out, which we hardly do anyway. If they made a course compulsory I'd do it, but I wouldn't put my hand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, yes. Like when you hear a new noise in the car and you turn the radio up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not put your hand up for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the young ones put their hand up and then they're the ones they send to the new line, and the new line closes a year later. Better to be steady and boring. Boring keeps its job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it came to it, where would you look for other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother-in-law Viktor has a removals van. He's said before I could help him on Saturdays. I'd think about that before anything with a computer.

S1.say: It's business: companies have to keep up or close, and then everyone's out. He wouldn't make a public fuss and doesn't want bosses to remember him as trouble.
S1.think: The wet end is the kind of work a computer could watch better than he does, and he's about average. If two out of five are cut, he doesn't know which side he's on.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and waits to see what the company actually does. Cancels satellite TV, takes a course only if it's compulsory, and considers Saturday work in his brother-in-law's removals van.
S1.feel: Anxious, like hearing a new noise in the car and turning the radio up.
S1.quote: Like when you hear a new noise in the car and you turn the radio up.
S1.fieldNote: Carlos describes his own avoidance with a lot of self-awareness. He believes staying steady and unremarkable is safer than volunteering for change, based on what he's seen. His fallback is family manual work, not anything digital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. I'd probably say nothing, or say it'll never happen here, because people say that to get through the day. Maybe I'd say the government needs to do something, everyone would be saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be finished there. A corrugator is just a long machine with sensors on it, they'd have it running by itself in no time. And two years, I'd have nothing saved, nothing learned, nowhere to go. I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop everything but the mortgage and food, that's the first thing. I'd go round to Viktor and ask him for proper work, not Saturdays, and we might have to move into my mother's flat if the house went. I'd look at the warehouses on the motorway, but they'd be going robot too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like being in a lift when the cable snaps, you just drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Viktor's van really hold two families?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two jobs, him and me, on one van, in a world where robots move furniture too? It's a dream, I know. But you grab what's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nikolai first. He's fifteen, he'd understand. I'd tell him straight, we're in trouble, I need you to help your mother. Katya's eleven, I'd just tell her we're having a quiet year.

S2.say: He doesn't know what he'd say; probably nothing, or that it'll never happen here, because people say that to get through the day. Maybe that the government needs to do something.
S2.think: He'd be finished at the plant, because a corrugator is just a long machine with sensors and could run itself quickly. With two years he'd have nothing saved, nothing learned and nowhere to go.
S2.do: Stops all spending except mortgage and food, asks his brother-in-law Viktor for full-time removals work and considers moving into his mother's flat if the house goes. Looks at motorway warehouses while knowing they'd automate too.
S2.feel: Sick, like being in a lift when the cable snaps.
S2.quote: Like being in a lift when the cable snaps, you just drop.
S2.fieldNote: Carlos has no plan in this picture and admits it; even his public line is uncertain. His options are all family-based and he knows they may not hold. The easy-going manner from the calmer pictures is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so we'd better be ready, but I wouldn't know what ready looks like. I'd listen more than I'd talk. Somebody at work would have an opinion, they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be forty-eight. Too old to start over easily, too young to stop. The plant would probably keep me till the last couple of years, I think, because changing the corrugator costs a lot. Then I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put money aside every month, even a little, which we've never managed. I'd talk to Nikolai about not going into a factory, maybe something with people, I don't know what. And I'd wait and see what the plant does, because I still don't trust anything until it's in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slower. Like the lift is going down floor by floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying wait and see. Is that a plan, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I know. Elena would say exactly that. But changing what I do when I don't know what to change to, that's how you lose money you haven't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having the five years help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. You'd have a few years to see what other people do. If the man next door found something that worked, I'd copy him.

S3.say: It's coming, so people had better be ready, but he wouldn't know what ready looks like. He'd listen more than talk.
S3.think: At 48 he'd be too old to start over easily and too young to stop. He expects the plant to keep him until the last couple of years because changing the corrugator is expensive, then he's out.
S3.do: Tries to save a little every month for the first time. Steers his son away from factory work and waits to see what the plant does before changing anything himself.
S3.feel: Alarmed, but more slowly, like a lift going down floor by floor.
S3.quote: Too old to start over easily, too young to stop.
S3.fieldNote: When challenged, Carlos defends waiting as protecting money he doesn't have. Five years only slows his fall, in his own image of the lift. He would copy a neighbour who found something that worked rather than lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. Probably they'll find something for people to do. That's what I'd say at work, and I'd mostly believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and I'm fifty-three, the house nearly paid, the kids grown. I could do another job at the end, driving or labouring, if there's still any. I wouldn't be happy, but I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep working, pay a bit extra on the mortgage when we can. Make sure the kids finish school and find something. I'm not going to start studying at forty-three, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in the background, but I can live with it. Like an old knee, it aches but you walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would there still be driving or labouring work, if robots can do almost any work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same question, I know. If robots can do almost everything, maybe there's nothing. But in ten years the government will have to have a plan, there'll be too many people like me for them to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your plan sounds like waiting for others to sort it out. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would worry me, a little. I'd want someone at work talking for us. I don't want to be the one doing it, but I'd sign.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen; they'll probably find something for people to do. He'd mostly believe that himself.
S4.think: At 53 he'd have the house nearly paid and the children grown, and could take a driving or labouring job if any are left. He wouldn't be happy but would be all right.
S4.do: Keeps working and pays a bit extra on the mortgage when possible. Makes sure the children finish school, and won't start studying at his age.
S4.feel: A background worry he can live with, like an old knee that aches while he keeps walking.
S4.quote: Like an old knee, it aches but you walk.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Carlos fall back on his preferred approach of carrying on. He hopes government will act because too many people will be affected, but he wouldn't lead anything himself. He'd sign a petition, not organise it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help, really, is time, and some money to bridge it. If they gave people a year's pay to find something, people like me could think straight. And a person to talk to, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the plant. If it went, the whole street would feel it, the café, the bakery, the bus. It's not just me.

headlineQuote: I don't use any of this AI on my phone, my son tried to show me once and I told him I've got enough things talking to me.
portrait: Carlos Petrov is 43 and has run the wet end of a corrugator at a cardboard box plant for sixteen years, living with his wife Elena, who works part-time in a pharmacy, and their two children on almost no savings. He never uses AI and prefers to stay steady and unremarkable at work, wary of volunteering for anything new. He is calm about a plateau and anxious about steady change, but two-year AGI leaves him panicked, with only family options like his brother-in-law's removals van. With more time he falls back on waiting, small savings and paying down the mortgage, hoping government will act. He blames no one in particular and sees it all as business.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd have nothing saved, nothing learned and nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: Time and money to bridge it, such as a year's pay to find something else, and a real person to talk to rather than a website.
